The word scuttlebutt has two meanings — one old and literal, one modern and figurative. You need to know both, because one gave birth to the other.

Meaning 1 — The Literal, Historical One: A Water Barrel on a Ship

Long ago, on sailing ships, sailors got their drinking water from a large wooden barrel kept on the ship's deck. That barrel was called a scuttlebutt. Think of it as the ship's water fountain.

Sailors would walk up to this barrel throughout the day to take a drink. And naturally, while standing there, they would chat — about the captain, about the journey, about rumors they'd heard below deck. It was the one place where everyone gathered informally.

This is important because it explains everything about the second meaning.

Meaning 2 — The Modern, Everyday One: Gossip or Rumor

Today, when someone says scuttlebutt, they almost always mean gossip, rumors, or unofficial talk — especially the kind that spreads informally among a group of people.

It refers to information that:

  • Has not been officially confirmed
  • Is passed from person to person through casual conversation
  • May or may not be true

Think of it as "word on the street," "talk going around," or "what people are whispering about." The connection to the water barrel makes perfect sense: just like sailors gossiped at the ship's water barrel, modern people gossip at the office water cooler, in hallways, or in group chats.
The Core Idea to Hold Onto

Scuttlebutt = informal, unverified talk or rumors circulating among a group of people.

It doesn't mean outright lies. It doesn't mean confirmed facts either. It sits right in between — the kind of information people share before it's been officially announced or proven. It has a slightly playful, informal feel.
How It's Used in Real Life

Here are clear examples to show you exactly how the word works:

  • "The scuttlebutt around the office is that the manager is quitting."
    → People are talking about it, but nobody has confirmed it officially.
  • "Don't believe everything you hear — that's just scuttlebutt."
    → Someone is warning you that the information is just gossip, not fact.
  • "I heard some interesting scuttlebutt about the new project."
    → The speaker picked up some unofficial, informal information.
  • "What's the scuttlebutt?"
    → A casual way of asking: "What are people saying? What's the gossip?"

1. It is always informal.
You would never use this word in a formal report or a professional document. It belongs in casual speech and informal writing.

2. It implies uncertainty.
When you call something "scuttlebutt," you are signaling that the information has not been verified. You are not presenting it as a confirmed fact. This is a crucial part of the word's meaning.

3. It is not necessarily negative.
Unlike the word "gossip," which sometimes has a mean-spirited or harmful tone, "scuttlebutt" is generally neutral or even lighthearted. It just means informal talk that's going around — it doesn't imply that anyone is being cruel or malicious.

4. It is often used in group settings.
Scuttlebutt tends to refer to rumors circulating within a community — a workplace, a military unit, a neighborhood, a school. It's the kind of talk that spreads through a shared group, not just between two private individuals.

5. It is a mass noun.
Like the word "gossip," you don't typically say "a scuttlebutt" or "scuttlebutts" (plural) when using it in the figurative sense. You say "some scuttlebutt," "the scuttlebutt," or just "scuttlebutt."

If you had to boil it down to one sentence:

Scuttlebutt is the unofficial, unverified talk and rumors that circulate informally among a group of people.

That's the word, fully and completely. You now know both what it means, what it implies, how it feels in tone, and how to use it correctly.
